newsitem.title: USA: Miami takeover not imminent, governor's aide says.
newsitem.headline: Miami takeover not imminent, governor's aide says.

text.p: Miami's declaration of a financial emergency does not mean a state takeover is imminent, but does pave the way for such a move if necessary, a spokeswoman for Gov. Lawton Chiles said Wednesday.

"The mayor basically told the governor that they meet the criteria for financial emergency. This does not mean that the state will take over," spokeswoman Karen Pankowski said. "It means the governor has certain authorities and we have some options."
The declaration could allow the governor to appoint a financial emergency board to take over fiscal management of the city, something no Florida governor has ever done.
Pankowsi said state officials were reviewing how other states had handled in similar situations.
"We've obviously never had anything quite like this in Florida," she said.

Mayor Joe Carollo met with Chiles in Tallahassee late Tuesday, and later told the Miami Herald that he would welcome a state takeover. He said they discussed the possibility of declaring bankruptcy but that the move would be premature.
John Incorvaia, a vice president at Moody's Investors Service, agreed bankruptcy would be premature but said it was significant that the mayor had uttered the word publicly for the first time.
"We agree with them," Incorvaia said. "But we needed to point out to people that now they're starting to refer to the word 'bankruptcy' and that's always a concern."
Pankowski and Incorvaia said the city had not provided an updated estimate of its deficit, which Carollo said was larger than the previously disclosed $68 milliom.

However, Incorvaia said, "We always realized the $68 million wasn't an exact science. It could have been a little higher, a little lower. We realize that was a developing situation and tha the number might move a little bit."
Miami City Commissioners are scheduled to vote Dec 12 on a bailout plan that includes major fee increases and concessions from its employee unions.

"Some politically hard decisions are gong to have to be made over the next month or so," Incorvaia said. "Even though the word 'bankruptcy' has been mentioned and is always a viable action, we're still looking for them to try to solve the situation."
